title: Jeremiah 5:10–19
context: Jeremiah 5:10–19 continues the LORD’s words. He commands attackers to go up on Jerusalem’s walls and destroy, but not to make a full end. The people have denied the LORD, saying that disaster will not come and that the prophets are only wind. The LORD answers that he will make his words in Jeremiah’s mouth a fire and the people wood. He will bring a nation from far away, ancient and mighty, whose language they do not know, which will eat their harvest, flocks, vines, and cities. Yet even then, he says, he will not make a full end of them. When they ask why, they will be told that because they served foreign gods in their own land, they will serve strangers in a land not theirs. The nation is not named here; later in the book the enemy from the north is identified with Babylon (25:9). Both traditions treat the promise not to make a full end as shared ground about judgment and remnant.

verses.text: “Go up on her walls, and destroy, but don’t make a full end. Take away her branches, for they are not the LORD’s.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands attackers to go up on Jerusalem’s walls and destroy, but not make a full end, and to strip away branches that are not his. Arminians see judgment that is real but limited, leaving room for a remnant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign control over the extent of judgment. Both traditions hold the promise not to make a full end as shared ground, which returns in verse 18 and points to God’s purpose of preserving a remnant.

verses.text: For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have dealt very treacherously against me,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that both the house of Israel and the house of Judah have dealt very treacherously with him. Arminian readers see the whole covenant people named, since Judah had followed the northern kingdom’s unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see treachery as the betrayal of a covenant relationship. Both traditions note that the northern kingdom had already fallen to Assyria (2 Kings 17), and that Judah is now warned not to repeat its path.

verses.text: They have denied the LORD, and said, “It is not he. Evil won’t come on us. We won’t see sword or famine.
verses.arminianNotes: The people deny the LORD and say that disaster will not come and they will not see sword or famine. Arminians see false confidence that refuses to believe God’s warnings, which is a form of practical unbelief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the denial as rejecting God’s word through his prophets. Both traditions note that the people’s words show they did not take God’s justice seriously, and they read the verse as the people’s claim, not the truth.

verses.text: The prophets will become wind, and the word is not in them. Thus it will be done to them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people say the prophets will become wind and the word is not in them. Arminian readers see contempt for God’s messengers, which leads the people to dismiss warnings they did not want to hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Both traditions note the wordplay, since the Hebrew word for wind can also mean spirit, and they read the verse as the people’s mockery of the true prophets, which God answers in the next verse.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD, the God of Armies says, “Because you speak this word, behold, I will make my words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it will devour them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says that because they speak this way, he will make his words in Jeremiah’s mouth fire and the people wood, and it will consume them. Arminians see God’s word as powerful and effective, carrying out the judgment it announces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s word as accomplishing his purpose. Both traditions note that God’s answer to the mockery of verse 13 is that his word through Jeremiah is not wind but fire, and they compare the commission in 1:9.

verses.text: Behold, I will bring a nation on you from far away, house of Israel,” says the LORD. “It is a mighty nation. It is an ancient nation, a nation whose language you don’t know and don’t understand what they say.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will bring a nation from far away, mighty and ancient, whose language the people do not know. Arminian readers see the coming invader, which later chapters identify with Babylon (25:9), though the nation is not named here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over the nations. Both traditions note the echo of the covenant warnings in Deuteronomy 28:49, and they treat the foreign language as one sign of how strange and overwhelming the judgment will be.

verses.text: Their quiver is an open tomb. They are all mighty men.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the invaders’ quiver is an open tomb and they are all mighty men. Arminians see a striking image of the deadly power of the coming army, whose arrows bring death wherever they fly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the image as stressing the certainty of the danger. Both traditions treat the verse as poetic description of the enemy, without trying to identify specific weapons or battles.

verses.text: They will eat up your harvest and your bread, which your sons and your daughters should eat. They will eat up your flocks and your herds. They will eat up your vines and your fig trees. They will beat down your fortified cities in which you trust with the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: The invaders will eat up the harvest, children’s food, flocks, herds, vines, fig trees, and fortified cities. Arminian readers see the total loss that would come on the land, and they note that the people trusted in their walls rather than in God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the repeated words eat up as stressing complete devastation. Both traditions note the echo of covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:31–33) and read the fortified cities as a false object of trust.

verses.text: “But even in those days,” says the LORD, “I will not make a full end of you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that even in those days he will not make a full end of them. Arminians see God’s mercy within judgment, preserving a people even when most of the nation suffers for its unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness to his covenant purposes, which ensures that a remnant remains. Both traditions treat this as shared ground about judgment and remnant, and they connect it with later promises of restoration in the book (compare 30:11).

verses.text: It will happen when you say, ‘Why has the LORD our God done all these things to us?’ Then you shall say to them, ‘Just as you have forsaken me and served foreign gods in your land, so you will serve strangers in a land that is not yours.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that when the people ask why he has done this, they will be told that as they served foreign gods in their own land, they will serve strangers in a land not theirs. Arminians see a fitting judgment, where the punishment matches the sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the correspondence between sin and judgment as showing God’s justice. Both traditions note that the verse anticipates the exile in Babylon, and they read its answer as God explaining his actions rather than leaving the people in confusion.
